title: Get it wrong and you spoil something
intro: Chronological order gives away a twist, a reveal or an ending the films were built around. Watch these in release order the first time.

franchises.why: Starting with the prequels tells you who Luke's father is six hours before Luke finds out.
Made in a scrambled order on purpose. Straightened out, it becomes a different and far plainer story.
The original five form a time loop, so any chronological start is arbitrary, and it gives away the most famous ending in sci-fi.
Saw III and IV end on the same moment from different angles. The reveals only land in the order they were made.
Final Destination 5 ends by leading straight into the first film. Watch it first and the twist is gone.
Part Three resolves the whole trilogy back in 1994. Starting in 1666 hands you the ending.
Watch the prequel first and Snow is a tragedy. Watch it last and he's a monster whose origins you finally understand.
The Beginning explains the scar the whole series keeps referring to. Watching it last is the intended experience.
Fantastic Beasts assumes you already know who Dumbledore and Grindelwald are. Chronologically right, dramatically backwards.
Days of Future Past resets the timeline. The reset only means something if you've watched what it erases.
Captain Marvel and The First Avenger make a slow start, and the Infinity Saga was built to be followed as it came out.
The prequel is written for people who already know how the first film ends.
Cube Zero explains the cube. The original is at its best with no explanation at all.
Rise of the Lycans shows what the first two films reveal in flashback. Save it, then rewatch chronologically: the war is easier to follow.
Lightyear is the film Andy watched in 1995. It makes almost no sense if you haven't met Buzz yet.
Prometheus explains what Alien wisely leaves unexplained. Meet the creature first.

title: Where chronological order wins
intro: The rare cases where following the story's own timeline is the better watch, even first time round.

franchises.why: Tokyo Drift belongs after Fast & Furious 6. Watched there, Han's fate lands as the series intended.
The 2009 film branches into its own timeline, and the three Kelvin films are the easiest way in for a newcomer.
The Last Key ends minutes before the first film begins. An unusually smooth run for a series that arrived this out of order.
Part 3 picks up the day after the first film ends, so it belongs before Part 2.
Ballerina runs alongside Chapter 3, so it fits neatly before Chapter 4.
Skull Island introduces the organisation that runs through everything else. It works perfectly first.

title: There is no single order
intro: Reboots, remakes and sequels that ignore each other. Choose a timeline and stick to it.

franchises.why: The 2018 film ignores everything after 1978, H20 ignores 4 to 6, Rob Zombie remade it, and Halloween III has no Michael Myers at all.
Two origin stories for the same killer, and two sequels to the 1974 film that ignore each other.
Dark Fate follows Judgment Day and ignores the three films between. For one clean story: 1, 2, Dark Fate.
George Miller calls them legends retold, not a fixed sequence. Only Furiosa's place is certain.
Bumblebee contradicts the 2007 film. Whether it's a prequel or a soft reboot has never been settled.
The Beginning and Dominion are two cuts of the same prequel. Believer ignores everything after 1973.
Rasen and Ring 2 are rival sequels to the same film. You only need one.
Manhunter and Red Dragon adapt the same novel. Choose one, and Hannibal Rising is easily skipped.
The Flash scrambles its own timeline and the line was retired soon after. Any chronology is a best reading.
The Paradox implies the creatures leaked across time. The chronology is deliberately unresolved.
Two separate pairs: the 1989 film and its sequel, and the 2019 remake and its prequel.
Mufasa is a prequel to the 2019 remake, not the 1994 film. 1½ retells the original from Timon and Pumbaa's side.
The 2016 film stands alone. Afterlife picks up from Ghostbusters II, thirty-two years later.
Only the two del Toro films share a continuity. The rest each start again.
Four actors, three continuities. Shadow Recruit sits first by story only because it restarts with a younger Ryan.
The series never kept a consistent timeline, and the 2021 film is an unrelated reboot.

title: It barely matters
intro: The order differs on paper, but nothing big is lost either way. Where we lean one way, we say so.

franchises.why: Spin-offs reach back to the 1950s, but each film stands up on its own.
Pearl is the origin of X's villain and works well before or after.
Day One expands a flashback from Part II. It works in either position.
Prey is set in 1719 and needs nothing else. It's a fine first film or a fine fifth.
The First Purge shows the original experiment. A good opener if you already know the premise.
The Hobbit first is fine for children, but the Rings trilogy is the reason anyone comes back.
The First Omen leads straight into the 1976 film and lands harder once you've seen it.
Temple of Doom is a prequel, but Raiders is the better introduction to Indy.
The prequel reading is a popular fan theory, not something the films say.
The first two films interlock rather than follow each other. Release order is the simplest path.
The Scorpion King expands a character from The Mummy Returns. Meet him there first.
The King's Man is far more serious than the others. Starting there misrepresents the series.
Puss in Boots is a prequel, but he works best introduced in Shrek 2.
Minions is first by story, but the joke works better once you know the Minions.
Destroy All Monsters is set in 1999, so it moves to the end. Nothing else changes.
Only the three Venom films need to be watched in order.
The Legend Begins follows an ancestor. A curiosity, not an opener.
Parts 2 and 3 are a separate story set in 1431.
WXIII sits between the first two films and barely features the main cast.
Only Jason X moves, and only because it's set in 2455.
New Nightmare is set in the real world, outside the story.
The prequel recasts both leads, and the sequel ignores it.
Origin of Evil stands alone and is the one to watch if you only watch one.
University works first, though the original assumes you're meeting them for the first time.
